what_its_for: Sargramostim is a man-made form of a protein that helps your body make more white blood cells. It is used to help your immune system recover after bone marrow transplants, chemotherapy, or stem cell transplants. It can also help reduce the risk of serious infections when your white blood cell count is very low.
how_to_take: Sargramostim is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a vein (intravenous infusion). A healthcare provider will usually give you this medicine in a clinic or hospital. If your doctor teaches you to give it at home, always follow their exact instructions. Use a new needle and syringe each time and never reuse them. Rotate injection sites to avoid soreness. Do not shake the vial — gently swirl it if needed.
dosing: Your dose is based on your body weight and the condition being treated. The typical dose is 250 micrograms per square meter of body surface area given once daily. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and how many days you need it. Always follow your doctor's specific dosing instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, contact your doctor or healthcare provider right away for instructions. Do not double up on your next dose to make up for a missed one. Since this medicine is often given in a clinical setting, your care team will help you stay on schedule.
storage: Store unopened vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep the vials in their original packaging to protect them from light. Once a vial has been opened, use it within 6 hours if kept at room temperature or within 24 hours if refrigerated. Throw away any unused medicine left in the vial — do not save it for later. Keep out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting vaccines without first checking with your doctor, as some vaccines may not be safe while you are taking this medicine. Try to avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, since your immune system may still be recovering. Avoid touching your eyes, nose, or mouth with unwashed hands. Do not use sargramostim if it looks cloudy, discolored, or contains particles.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience: sudden shortness of breath or trouble breathing, chest pain or a fast or irregular heartbeat, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat (signs of a serious allergic reaction), severe redness, rash, or hives, high fever or chills, unusual bleeding or bruising, severe pain at the injection site, or feeling faint or dizzy. Also call your doctor if you develop any new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: Sargramostim usually starts to work within a few days of starting treatment. Your doctor will monitor your white blood cell counts with regular blood tests to see how well the medicine is working. Most people start to see their white blood cell counts rise within 7 to 14 days. Your doctor will let you know when your counts are in a safe range.
special_populations: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding before using this medicine, as the risks are not fully known. Let your doctor know if you have a history of heart problems, lung disease, fluid retention, liver or kidney disease, or any autoimmune conditions. Older adults and people with certain health conditions may need closer monitoring. This medicine may be used in children, but the dose will be carefully adjusted by the doctor.
